paragraphs.heading: Wind you can see
paragraphs.text: The Beaufort scale, known in full as the Beaufort wind force scale, ties the speed of the wind to what an observer can see happening at sea or on land. It was never exact or objective: it grew out of people looking at a ship and at the water around it. Today forecasters usually give wind speed in kilometres or miles per hour, or in knots for ships and aircraft. Still, Beaufort terms turn up in forecasts for shipping and in severe weather warnings for the public.

paragraphs.heading: Why a standard was needed
paragraphs.text: In the 1700s, naval officers logged the weather regularly, but there was no shared scale, so their reports were very personal. What one officer called a stiff breeze, another might call a soft one. Francis Beaufort, a hydrographer in Britain's Royal Navy, worked out a standard scale in 1805 while serving on HMS Woolwich. It built on earlier efforts by others, including Daniel Defoe a century before. Its first use was aboard HMS Beagle, captained by Robert FitzRoy, on the "Darwin voyage" of 1831–1836.

paragraphs.heading: From sails to sea
paragraphs.text: The first version had 13 classes, numbered 0 to 12. Instead of giving wind speeds, it described what the wind did to the sails of a frigate, then the Royal Navy's main ship, from barely enough to steer by to more than any canvas could bear. In the late 1830s the Navy made it the standard for ships' logs, and in 1853 an international meteorological conference in Brussels accepted it for general use. In 1916, as steam power grew, the descriptions switched from the sails to the behaviour of the sea, and descriptions for land were added. A standard way of turning instrument readings into scale numbers came only in 1923, under George Simpson of the UK Meteorological Office.

paragraphs.heading: Numbers added later
paragraphs.text: The wind speeds that match each step were worked out after the scale existed, and those conversions have never been made official. One formula links the scale number to the wind speed 10 metres above the sea. By that formula, force 9.5 corresponds to 24.5 metres per second, which is where force 10 begins. The same formula would put the strongest hurricane winds at 23 on the scale.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond force 12
paragraphs.text: In 1946 the scale gained five more steps, forces 13 to 17, meant only for special cases such as tropical cyclones. Taiwan, mainland China and Vietnam, which typhoons often strike, use this longer version today. China switched to it without notice on the morning of 15 May 2006 and used it at once for Typhoon Chanchu. Hong Kong and Macau still stop at force 12. The World Meteorological Organization's 2012 manual for marine services also defined the scale only up to 12, with no advice on the extension.

paragraphs.heading: How warnings use it
paragraphs.text: The scale still shapes warnings in many places. BBC Radio 4's Shipping Forecasts in the United Kingdom use it, and Ireland's weather service, Met Éireann, issues a Small Craft Warning when force 6 winds are expected up to 10 nautical miles offshore. In the United States, force 6 or 7 brings a small craft advisory, while 8 or 9 calls for a gale warning, 10 or 11 for a storm warning, and 12 for a hurricane-force wind warning. Canada uses a similar ladder, in which forecast winds of 6 to 7 count as strong, 8 to 9 as gale force, 10 to 11 as storm force and 12 as hurricane force.
